newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: New Zealand says still uneasy about nuclear ship.
newsitem.headline: New Zealand says still uneasy about nuclear ship.

text.p: New Zealand on Thursday continued to express concern about the passage and safety of a Japan-bound ship carrying plutonium waste while Australia said it had been assured the ship would not pass through its waters.

New Zealand Foreign Minister Don McKinnon, in Australia to attend a regular meeting with his Australian counterpart Alexander Downer, said his country's view on the passage of the ship was "the further away (from New Zealand) the better".

Greenpeace environmental activitists have protested in New Zealand at the planned route through the southwest Pacific of the British ship Pacific Teal, carrying cycled nuclear waste from France to Japan and Malaysia has banned it from its waters.
The recycled wasted is being shipped back to Japan after being reprocessed in France.

McKinnon said New Zealand could only assume that the ship would go through the Tasman Sea, which separates his country and Australia, and hoped to get an undertaking from Japan that it would not traverse New Zealand's 200 mile economic zone.
"But we are concerned about the safety, the liability of the carrier, and preferably, we would rather it did not come," he told a news conference after meeting Downer here.
McKinnon said there had been more than 150 similar shipments between France and Japan, raising concern in his country "given the attitude of most New Zealanders to nuclear issues".
New Zealand braved anger from the United States in the 1980s by banning nuclear-powered and nuclear-armed ships from its waters, and forms part of a self-declared nuclear free zone in the Pacific.
However, McKinnon said the shipments like the Pacific Teal were governed by international maritime rights.
"Ultimately we hope the Japanese could reprocess their own nuclear waste and that would enable the material not to have to travel anywhere," he said.
Downer said the Australian government had been assured by Japan, France, and Britain that the ship's planned route would not entail passage through Australian territorial waters.
Australia also had been given assurances the ship's radiological protection and safety arrangements met international standards, he said.
"We are satisfied they do meet international standards but obviously this is a shipment that has to be handled with great sensitivity on all of their parts," Downer said.
